orientation: AI product engineering starts with a useful decision. A baseline is the simple existing approach that a new system must improve.
idea: Choose the decision and cost of being wrong before choosing the model.
story: Meera handles equipment-rental messages. Her manager asks for an AI assistant, but the immediate problem is smaller: urgent breakdown reports wait behind routine return questions. The user job is to get each ticket to the right queue quickly.

A keyword rule looks for “broken”. It is cheap and understandable, but “the drill stopped working” slips through. A model may help with phrasing; that still does not prove it reduces the expensive misses. First compare both on the same labelled tickets.
example: On a fictional batch of 20 tickets, a rule gets 18 routes right but misses 2 urgent cases. A model gets 19 right and misses 1 urgent case. That is a useful lead, not proof of readiness: inspect which case failed and test more representative messages.
trap: A fluent reply is not evidence of correct routing. Judge the action the support desk needs, including the mistakes it cannot afford.

lab.question: Which approach best fits a desk that cannot afford missed breakdown reports?
lab.limitation: Fixed synthetic case explorer: these are invented routing outcomes for the same 20 tickets, not a running rule engine or model benchmark.

scenarios.label: 1 · Keyword rule
scenarios.result: The rule misses two urgent tickets.
scenarios.why: Overall accuracy hides which errors hurt the desk; review the two missed breakdowns.

scenarios.label: 2 · Mock model
scenarios.result: The mock model improves this batch but still misses one urgent case.
scenarios.why: One additional correct route is evidence about these fixtures only; deployment needs a defined acceptance rule.

scenarios.label: 3 · Route all urgent
scenarios.result: No urgent case is missed, but the urgent queue is flooded.
scenarios.why: A one-sided metric can reward a useless system. Track false alarms and handling capacity alongside missed urgent cases.

mechanism: Write one sentence naming the person, decision and benefit: “Help a support agent route urgent breakdowns promptly.” This keeps the evaluation tied to a real workflow.
Compare a manual or rules baseline and the candidate on the same inputs. Record costly error types separately; a single average can hide an unacceptable tradeoff.
Choose an acceptance boundary before inspecting results. If evidence is too limited, retain human triage and collect more labelled cases instead of treating a demo as a release decision.

transfer.question: An assistant writes beautiful refund replies but still sends tickets to the wrong team. Has it solved this lesson’s user job?
transfer.answer: No. Writing quality is a different outcome from correct routing. Measure routing and its consequences, or explicitly redefine the job.

transfer.question: The model wins on all 20 fixtures. Does that prove it will win next month?
transfer.answer: No. The fixtures may omit new wording, languages or rare urgent events. They support a bounded observation, not a guarantee.

checks.question: What should be written first?
options: The user decision and success measure
A prompt for every possible ticket
checks.explanation: The decision determines what to measure and whether a model is needed.

checks.question: Why is 95% correct insufficient by itself?
options: The remaining errors may be disproportionately costly
checks.explanation: The kind and consequence of the errors matter, as well as their count.

checks.question: What makes a fair baseline comparison?
options: Use easier tickets for the model
Use the same representative cases and decision criteria
checks.explanation: Changing the cases or criteria confounds the comparison.

topics.title: user jobs
topics.explanation: A user job describes progress someone needs to make, not a feature name. “Route a broken drill report quickly” is more testable than “add AI to support”.

topics.title: failure costs
topics.explanation: Different mistakes consume different resources or cause different harm. A routine ticket in the urgent queue costs attention; an urgent ticket in the routine queue delays help, so count both separately.

topics.title: rules versus ML versus generation
topics.explanation: Rules encode explicit conditions, ML learns patterns, and generation produces content. A fixed return-date calculation may need only rules, while varied wording may justify a classifier; generating a paragraph does not automatically improve either decision.

topics.title: baseline
topics.explanation: A baseline is a simple comparison point with measured behaviour. Keep its inputs and scoring aligned with the candidate, and include the current human workflow where relevant.

sources.title: Full Stack Deep Learning: when to use ML

steps: Create six fictional tickets: two obvious breakdowns, two indirect breakdowns and two routine questions. Label the desired queue before testing your rule.
Apply a keyword rule and record missed urgent cases and unnecessary urgent routes separately. Ask a second person to challenge ambiguous labels if available.
Write a three-sentence decision brief naming the user, acceptance boundary and one reason to keep human triage.

orientation: A quality metric scores system behaviour. A business metric measures whether the workflow helps, while unit economics asks what one useful outcome costs.
idea: Count the full cost per successful outcome, including human review and failures.
story: Meera’s rental desk receives a proposal: an assistant that costs only ₹2 per ticket. The quote sounds attractive, until she learns that some replies need a staff review and some still fail to resolve the request.

She writes down the denominator: successfully resolved cases. Paying less for each attempted answer can still cost more for each resolution. Now she can compare alternatives using the same fictional batch and a clearly stated success definition.
example: For 100 attempts, model calls cost 100 × ₹2 = ₹200. Reviewing 20 replies costs 20 × ₹15 = ₹300. Total cost is ₹500. If 80 cases are resolved, cost per resolution is ₹500 ÷ 80 = ₹6.25. Unresolved cases still contributed to the bill.
trap: Do not divide only by generated replies and call it cost per resolution. An attempted response, a reviewed response and a resolved customer problem are different events.

lab.question: How does review burden change cost per resolved rental-support case?
lab.limitation: Fixed synthetic case explorer: all prices and resolution counts are invented. This is accounting over fixed scenarios, not a pricing quote or a live forecast.

scenarios.label: 1 · Light review
scenarios.result: Total cost is ₹500 for 80 resolutions.
scenarios.why: The numerator includes costs of unresolved attempts too. These figures exclude fixed engineering and support costs.

scenarios.label: 2 · Heavy review
scenarios.result: The same 80 resolutions now cost ₹800.
scenarios.why: Review doubled, even though resolution count did not improve. Lower model-call prices alone would miss this cost driver.

scenarios.label: 3 · Fewer resolutions
scenarios.result: The same ₹500 spend now costs ₹10 per resolution.
scenarios.why: The denominator fell. Measuring only spend per attempted ticket would hide the deterioration.

mechanism: Define “resolved” before counting. For this toy desk, a staff-labelled case is resolved only if the reply correctly settles the customer’s issue; sending text is not enough.
List variable costs over the same period: model calls, review and rework. Add fixed development and operating costs for a full decision, with an explicit allocation assumption.
Set both quality and operational acceptance criteria. A cheaper workflow that mishandles urgent breakdowns can fail the release gate even when its average cost looks good.

transfer.question: A new model halves call cost to ₹100, but review rises to ₹600 and only 50 cases resolve. Is it cheaper than the baseline scenario?
transfer.answer: No. Its stated cost is ₹700 / 50 = ₹14 per resolution, versus ₹6.25. Other uncounted costs could change both totals further.

transfer.question: Does the cheapest scenario necessarily deserve release?
transfer.answer: No. It must also meet quality, capacity and user-outcome criteria. The fixed examples do not measure those criteria for a real service.

checks.question: Which denominator matches cost per resolution?
checks.explanation: Use the outcome named by the metric; unsuccessful attempts still cost money.

checks.question: What happened between light and heavy review?
options: Review cost rose without more resolutions
checks.explanation: Both have 100 calls and 80 resolutions, but review costs rise from ₹300 to ₹600.

checks.question: Which statement is an acceptance criterion?
options: At least 90 of 100 preselected routine cases must resolve correctly
checks.explanation: It names observable behaviour and a threshold. The threshold remains a fictional example, not a universal target.

topics.title: acceptance criteria
topics.explanation: Acceptance criteria specify observable conditions for deciding whether a change is acceptable. “No unsupported promises in the test fixtures” is inspectable; “the bot feels smart” is not.

topics.title: quality metrics
topics.explanation: Quality metrics describe output behaviour, such as correct routing or supported answers. Always state the sample and denominator; a score on routine cases says little about rare urgent reports.

topics.title: business metrics
topics.explanation: Business metrics track outcomes such as resolution time or repeat contacts. They can move differently from answer accuracy because review effort and workflow friction also affect users.

topics.title: unit economics
topics.explanation: Unit economics assigns costs and value to one meaningful unit. Include review and unsuccessful attempts in the numerator, and distinguish variable operating cost from total cost including development.

steps: Copy the cost table and calculate total variable cost and cost per resolved case for each row. State that all prices are hypothetical.
Add a scenario with 0 resolutions and explain why cost per resolution is undefined rather than zero.
Write one measurable quality gate and one business gate; explain why passing only the cost gate is insufficient.

orientation: Human control means giving people useful ways to clarify, correct or take over. Abstaining means declining to make an unsupported claim; escalation hands the case to someone able to act.
idea: Match the assistant’s action to the evidence and make recovery easy.
story: A customer asks Meera’s rental assistant when a replacement drill will arrive. The order has two addresses and no confirmed dispatch scan. “Tomorrow” would sound helpful, but the assistant does not yet have the facts to promise it.

The useful next action is to ask which address applies. If the carrier records later conflict, the assistant should explain the uncertainty and pass the case to dispatch, carrying the order context so the customer need not repeat everything.
example: One order has a confirmed carrier date, one lacks a delivery address, and one has conflicting tracking records. The appropriate paths are answer with its source, ask a focused question, and hold the promise while escalating. The same friendly tone can accompany all three paths.
trap: A confident voice or a self-reported “95% sure” is not verified evidence. Show what supports the answer and give the customer a practical correction path.

lab.question: What should the assistant do before promising a replacement delivery date?
lab.limitation: Fixed synthetic case explorer: the evidence and chosen policy paths are authored examples, not a live assistant or a calibrated uncertainty model.

scenarios.label: 1 · Verified date
scenarios.result: Answer: “The carrier currently lists 14 Oct.”
scenarios.why: A sourced current estimate can be useful without becoming a guarantee. Keep the correction and contact paths available.

scenarios.label: 2 · Missing address
scenarios.result: Ask which saved address should receive the replacement.
scenarios.why: The customer can supply the missing fact. Asking is more useful than guessing or escalating every incomplete request.

scenarios.label: 3 · Conflicting dates
scenarios.result: Explain the conflict and send the case to dispatch.
scenarios.why: Both records exist, but their disagreement is unresolved. More records do not automatically mean stronger evidence.

mechanism: Start by separating missing information from conflicting information. A customer can clarify an address, while dispatch may need to investigate inconsistent carrier records.
Make the next action specific: answer the supported part, ask one useful question, abstain from the unsupported promise, or escalate with the relevant context. These actions can be combined.
Correction should change the workflow, not merely trigger an apology. After the customer fixes an address, confirm what changed and recheck the delivery estimate before sending a new promise.

transfer.question: The customer corrects “Tuesday” to “Thursday”, but the system still schedules Tuesday. Has it supported correction?
transfer.answer: No. The visible acknowledgement did not update the consequential state. Confirm the corrected value and verify the schedule before proceeding.

transfer.question: Should every uncertain request immediately go to a human?
transfer.answer: No. A focused clarification can resolve some gaps. Escalate when policy, authority or unresolved evidence requires it, and make that boundary explicit.

checks.question: Two records disagree about a delivery date. What is justified?
checks.explanation: Conflicting evidence needs reconciliation, not a confident guess.

checks.question: What makes a correction useful?
options: The relevant state and next action reflect it
checks.explanation: A correction must affect the outcome that matters to the customer.

checks.question: Which uncertainty can the customer often resolve directly?
options: Whether a hidden provider outage occurred
checks.explanation: Ask the person who can actually supply the missing information.

topics.title: uncertainty
topics.explanation: Uncertainty can come from missing facts, contradictory sources or imperfect predictions. Name the actual gap; an unvalidated confidence percentage does not resolve it.

topics.title: user expectations
topics.explanation: Tell users what the assistant can do and where its information comes from. A carrier estimate should not be presented as a guaranteed arrival time.

topics.title: correction
topics.explanation: Make mistaken inputs and outputs easy to correct. After an address correction, show the new address and recompute dependent decisions instead of preserving the old plan.

topics.title: abstention
topics.explanation: Abstention means withholding an unsupported conclusion. The assistant can still explain the gap and provide a next step, such as requesting an order number.

topics.title: escalation
topics.explanation: Escalation transfers the case to someone with suitable evidence or authority. Include context and a clear handoff state; silently placing a case in a queue is not the same as having a human resolve it.

sources.title: Microsoft HAX: scope services when in doubt

steps: Draw three boxes for answer, ask and escalate using the replacement-delivery scenario. Add the evidence needed to enter each box.
Write a customer correction and the exact state change it should cause. Include a confirmation message.
Walk through one unavailable-human case and define an honest waiting message plus an owner for follow-up.

orientation: A delivery boundary defines which actions a system may take. A staged rollout exposes a change gradually, with an owner and a way to stop future use.
idea: Release the smallest useful capability whose failures you can observe and contain.
story: Meera’s team can buy a hosted assistant or build a routing component. A working demo settles neither choice. Both options need support, data access, operating costs and a way to switch when requirements change.

They start with draft replies for a small staff group. Humans still decide what to send. This boundary helps them inspect mistakes before expanding authority, while recording that stopping the feature cannot recall a message already sent.
example: A pilot creates 20 reply drafts and sends none automatically. Staff reject 4 drafts before customers see them. If automatic sending had been enabled on the same fictional outputs, 4 unsuitable replies would have reached customers. The model output is unchanged; the release boundary changes exposure.
trap: “We can roll back the code” does not mean every consequence can be reversed. Disabling future sends does not erase messages already delivered.

lab.question: How does the same set of 20 drafts affect customers under different delivery boundaries?
lab.limitation: Fixed synthetic case explorer: these are assumed review decisions for invented drafts, not measured rollout safety or a real vendor comparison.

scenarios.label: 1 · Staff-only pilot
scenarios.result: The team can inspect failures without sending these drafts to customers.
scenarios.why: This tests draft usefulness, not the full customer workflow or the cost of sustained review.

scenarios.label: 2 · Approval gate
scenarios.result: Staff approval blocks four unsuitable drafts in this example.
scenarios.why: A human gate adds work and can itself fail. The zero here is a fixed fixture outcome, not a promise about reviewers.

scenarios.label: 3 · Auto-send
scenarios.result: Four unsuitable messages already reached customers.
scenarios.why: Stopping the feature contains future exposure; existing effects need a separate recovery plan.

mechanism: Compare build and buy against the same requirements: task quality, acceptable data handling, integration effort, total cost and who will operate the service. A vendor demo is only one input.
Define the release boundary in terms of permissions and users. “Draft for five trained staff” is more concrete than “small launch”, because it identifies what the system can actually do.
Choose a pilot gate and rollback owner before expansion. Monitor both output quality and the workflow; document how to disable future work and how to recover from actions already taken.

transfer.question: A hosted model becomes unavailable. Which preparation helps more: a favourite provider name or a tested fallback path?
transfer.answer: A tested fallback path. A stable application contract and retained input/output fixtures help evaluate another provider or return to manual work.

transfer.question: The draft-only pilot succeeds. Is automatic sending now proven safe?
transfer.answer: No. Automatic sending changes the authority boundary. Review-free operation needs its own evidence, monitoring and recovery design.

checks.question: What does a useful pilot boundary specify?
options: Users, allowed actions and stop conditions
checks.explanation: These details make the exposure and responsibility inspectable.

checks.question: What can code rollback usually not do by itself?
checks.explanation: External effects often require separate recovery even after software rollback.

checks.question: Which build-versus-buy claim is strongest?
options: Compare requirements, full costs and exit options
checks.explanation: Both choices carry integration and operating responsibilities; evaluate them for the actual workflow.

topics.title: build versus buy
topics.explanation: Building gives control but requires sustained engineering and operations. Buying can shorten integration work, but the team still owns customer outcomes and must evaluate the service against its requirements.

topics.title: feasibility
topics.explanation: Feasibility asks whether the necessary data, skills and operating conditions exist. A polished demo does not establish that daily latency, review capacity or quality targets can be met.

topics.title: vendor dependency
topics.explanation: Dependency grows when prompts, data formats and workflows assume one provider’s behaviour. Keep an explicit application contract and representative fixtures so replacement decisions can be tested rather than guessed.

topics.title: staged rollout
topics.explanation: A staged rollout expands exposure after predefined evidence gates. Draft-only, human-approved and automatic modes have different failure consequences, so passing one stage does not automatically justify the next.

steps: Write a one-page decision table comparing a hosted service, a self-operated component and a manual fallback using the same requirements.
Define a staff-only pilot with a named owner, allowed actions, 20 fixtures and a measurable go/no-go rule.
Simulate one bad already-sent reply: write both the disable procedure and the separate customer-recovery action.

orientation: A Python component is a reusable function or module with clear inputs and outputs. Reproducibility means another person can recreate its documented behaviour from the same code, environment and inputs.
idea: Make inputs, dependencies and failures visible instead of relying on notebook memory.
story: Meera normalizes ticket text in a notebook before routing it. One cell reads a global queue prefix left behind by an earlier experiment. The displayed result looks right, but restarting the notebook changes what happens.

She moves normalization into a function that receives both text and prefix. Now a colleague can see the whole contract. Type hints explain the expected values; explicit checks still need to reject invalid values at runtime.
example: With text “  Drill STOPPED  ” and prefix “urgent”, normalization produces “urgent:drill stopped”. Passing prefix “routine” intentionally changes the output. A hidden prefix makes this dependency easy to miss; a declared parameter makes it inspectable and testable in a clean process.
trap: A Python annotation such as text: str does not enforce the input type at runtime. Add validation where untrusted data enters, and preserve useful failure information.

lab.question: Can another developer explain this normalizer’s output without access to the old notebook session?
lab.limitation: Fixed synthetic case explorer: displayed outputs and failures are authored snapshots. This page does not execute Python or recreate an environment.

scenarios.label: 1 · Explicit inputs
scenarios.result: Both required fields are explicit valid strings.
scenarios.why: Given this fixture and function, the result can be reconstructed without notebook history.

scenarios.label: 2 · Hidden prefix
scenarios.result: The output depends on a value the caller cannot see.
scenarios.why: The text did not change; hidden configuration did. Pass the prefix explicitly and document its meaning.

scenarios.label: 3 · Hints alone
scenarios.result: The annotation does not reject 42 before the function runs.
scenarios.why: A boundary check could raise a clear TypeError instead of a later, less helpful method failure.

mechanism: Name each input and output, then isolate the transformation in a function. Keep environment access and network calls outside this small core where practical, so fixtures remain easy to reason about.
Validate external inputs deliberately and catch only failures you can handle. Returning an empty string for every exception hides whether a customer supplied bad data or the program is broken.
Record the Python version, dependency versions and configuration names with a clean reproduction command. Commit the code and fixtures, not secrets or the virtual environment directory.

transfer.question: Two developers use identical code but different dependency versions. Is identical behaviour established?
transfer.answer: No. Dependencies can change behaviour. Recreate the documented environment and compare the same fixtures before claiming reproduction.

transfer.question: Does locking dependencies guarantee identical results for every AI service?
transfer.answer: No. External APIs, hardware, random choices and changing data may also matter. State what the reproduction recipe controls and what it does not.

checks.question: Which change removes the hidden prefix dependency?
options: Pass prefix as a named input
Add a longer comment above the old cell
checks.explanation: A parameter exposes the dependency to callers and tests.

checks.question: What does text: str do by itself?
options: Describe the expected type for tools and readers
checks.explanation: Python does not enforce ordinary type annotations at runtime.

checks.question: Which item belongs in the repository?
options: A small fixture and reproduction instructions
checks.explanation: Commit the recipe and safe fixtures; recreate environments and supply secrets separately.

topics.title: Python types
topics.explanation: Types describe the kinds of values a function expects and returns. A static checker can flag misuse, but Python annotations alone do not validate an incoming JSON field.

topics.title: exceptions
topics.explanation: Exceptions report failures such as invalid input or unavailable files. Catch a specific failure when you have a recovery path; swallowing every exception can turn broken ticket processing into silent data loss.

topics.title: modules
topics.explanation: A module groups reusable Python definitions in a file. Move ticket normalization out of notebook execution order so another entry point can import it without repeating exploratory cells.

topics.title: environments
topics.explanation: A virtual environment isolates installed packages for a project. Recreate it from documented versions rather than checking its directory into Git; isolation alone does not pin dependencies.

topics.title: configuration
topics.explanation: Configuration holds choices that vary between runs, such as a queue prefix or endpoint. Make required values explicit and validate them at startup; secret values should not appear in committed fixtures or logs.

topics.title: Git
topics.explanation: Git records versions of tracked files so changes can be reviewed and compared. A commit identifies code, but untracked data, secrets and an undocumented runtime remain outside that reproducibility record.

steps: Save the starter as normalize.py and run it in a clean Python 3.12 environment. Record the interpreter version and command.
Add cases for whitespace, an empty prefix and integer input; specify which are accepted and which should raise a clear error.
Create a small README listing inputs, output and configuration. Inspect your proposed Git changes to exclude secrets and .venv.

orientation: NumPy stores numbers in arrays: ordered collections with a shape (the length of each axis) and a dtype (the stored value type). Here, one position means one rental. Start with M02-L01’s explicit input contract; now make the array shapes part of that contract.
idea: Match each rental’s days to its own daily rate, then verify the output shape and a hand-calculated cost before trusting the total.
story: Meera closes the equipment-rental desk with three SYNTHETIC bookings: a drill for 2 days at 12 fictional currency units per day, a sander for 4 days at 7, and a lamp for 3 days at 9. She wants one charge per booking. Think of two aligned ledger columns: day counts and daily rates. Multiplying across each row gives that rental’s cost.

She puts days [2, 4, 3] and rates [12, 7, 9] into separate one-dimensional NumPy arrays. Each has shape (3,), meaning one axis with three entries. The same position in each array must still identify the same rental; NumPy does not know the equipment names. A Python loop pairs the entries explicitly. Vectorization expresses the same work as days * rates, applying multiplication across the arrays.

Then Meera adds a column axis to days. Its shape becomes (3, 1), while rates stays (3,). NumPy accepts the multiplication, but now compares every day count with every rate. Each number resembles a reasonable rental charge. The ledger analogy stops here: NumPy aligns dimensions, not booking identities. Predict the number of outputs before choosing the cases below.
example: SYNTHETIC matched costs: drill 2 × 12 = 24; sander 4 × 7 = 28; lamp 3 × 9 = 27 fictional currency units. A loop and days * rates both return [24, 28, 27], shape (3,), with total 24 + 28 + 27 = 79. Rates are per day; multiplying by days gives the whole rental charge, not a daily rate.
trap: A successful operation can answer the wrong question. Shapes (3, 1) × (3,) produce (3, 3): nine pairwise costs instead of three matched costs. Even the first value, 24, is right. Check the entire first row and the output shape before summing; a plausible first cell is not enough.

lab.question: SYNTHETIC fixed fixtures: this page does not run NumPy in the browser. For Meera’s same three rentals, will each shape choice produce three matched costs, nine pairwise costs, or an error?
lab.limitation: SYNTHETIC fixed case explorer. Inputs, outputs and the failure shown here are authored fixtures, not browser-executed NumPy or production evidence. Bars count output entries on a shared 0–9 scale; zero after an error means no output, not a free rental. Run the separate data lab for executable evidence.

scenarios.label: 1 · SYNTHETIC matched rows
scenarios.result: Three matched costs; loop and vectorized total both equal 79 fictional currency units.
scenarios.why: Equal one-dimensional shapes pair the same positions. Check the sander: 4 days × 7 units/day = 28 units. This assumes both arrays preserve rental order.

scenarios.label: 2 · SYNTHETIC pairwise trap
scenarios.result: Nine plausible costs sum to 252 units, but Meera has only three bookings.
scenarios.why: Broadcasting aligns dimensions from the right; equal lengths or a length of 1 can expand. Here each day count meets all three rates. Row one is [24, 14, 18], not the drill’s single charge 24. Require matching one-dimensional inputs and rerun case 1; do not flatten the nine wrong charges.

scenarios.label: 3 · SYNTHETIC missing rate
evidence: ValueError; restore lamp rate 9, then rerun → total 79
scenarios.result: No costs are produced: the missing lamp rate makes the shapes incompatible.
scenarios.why: NumPy raises ValueError for these shapes; your calculator should reject them at its input boundary too. Do not truncate the loop or invent a zero rate. Recover the matched source rate and select case 1 to inspect the corrected result.

mechanism: Keep the meaning beside the shape. One axis of length three is (3,); three rows of one column is (3, 1). Broadcasting permits some unequal shapes, but our per-rental contract deliberately requires two equal one-dimensional arrays. Reject a column input even when NumPy could multiply it. Validate finite values before computing: NaN means not-a-number, and infinity is not a usable rate.

Compare the vectorized values with a loop and the hand calculation, not just with each other. Declare an absolute tolerance of 1e-9 fictional currency units and relative tolerance 0 for this tiny float64 fixture. A reduction combines values along an axis: costs.sum() turns [24, 28, 27] into 79. Reducing the wrong matrix just hides the extra combinations. Both implementations can agree while using incorrectly ordered rates.

Take away three habits: name each axis, reject shapes outside the business contract, and verify a row plus the output shape before reducing. Array means an ordered numeric collection; broadcasting aligns compatible dimensions; vectorization applies an operation across an array. In M02-L06, tables and join keys will help establish which rate belongs to which booking before we do this arithmetic.

transfer.question: A new SYNTHETIC booking sheet has days [5, 2] and matched rates [6, 11]. What output and shape should you expect? What if days is accidentally shaped (2, 1)?
transfer.answer: The matched output is [30, 22], shape (2,), total 52 units. A column-shaped day array multiplied by rates of shape (2,) gives [[30, 55], [12, 22]], shape (2, 2), total 119. Those extra cross-booking combinations are valid arithmetic but invalid billing.

transfer.question: Both arrays have shape (3,), and the loop agrees with vectorization. Does that prove the rates belong to the correct equipment?
transfer.answer: No. Shapes cannot check identity. With the same days [2, 4, 3] but reordered rates [7, 12, 9], both implementations return [14, 48, 27], total 89. Verify the booking-to-rate mapping and compare a known row. Neither agreement nor finite values alone establishes correct billing.

checks.question: Predict: days has shape (3, 1) and rates has shape (3,). What does days * rates produce?
checks.explanation: The trailing 1 expands across three rates, while the missing leading rate axis acts as length 1 and expands across three rentals. The result is (3, 3). Our billing contract should reject that input even though NumPy accepts it.

checks.question: A new SYNTHETIC rental fixture has days [1, 3] and rates [8, 5, 4]. What should a per-rental calculator do?
options: Use the first two rates and return [8, 15]
Reject the mismatch and recover the missing pairing
checks.explanation: Shapes (2,) and (3,) cannot broadcast. A zip-based loop would silently drop the third rate unless you check lengths first. Reject the mismatch; do not guess which rental or rate is missing.

checks.question: Meera sets trial = rates[:2], then trial[0] = 0. Why does the drill’s original rate change?
options: The basic slice is a view sharing the numeric storage
Every slice creates an independent copy
checks.explanation: Basic slicing returns a view. Assigning through trial changes rates too. Use rates[:2].copy() for an isolated experiment and test that the original stays unchanged; ordinary days * rates creates a separate result.

topics.title: NumPy arrays and dtypes
topics.explanation: A numeric ndarray has a shape and a common storage dtype. Use np.array([2, 4, 3], dtype=np.int64) for these whole-day counts and np.array([12, 7, 9], dtype=np.float64) for rates. A dtype describes representation, not units or validity. Fixed-width integers can overflow; floating-point amounts need declared comparison and rounding rules. Our small synthetic fixture is not a money-accounting policy.

topics.title: broadcasting
topics.explanation: Compare axis lengths from the right. Each pair must match or contain a 1; missing leading axes act as 1. Thus (3,) with (3,) gives three matched values, while (3, 1) with (3,) gives a 3 × 3 pairwise table. Lengths 3 and 2 cannot expand into one another. Broadcasting knows sizes, not rental identities.

topics.title: axis reductions
topics.explanation: An axis is a numbered dimension. A reduction such as sum combines values along the chosen dimension. For the pairwise table [[24, 14, 18], [48, 28, 36], [36, 21, 27]], sum(axis=1) removes the column axis and gives row totals [56, 112, 84]; sum(axis=0) removes the row axis and gives column totals [108, 63, 81]. Neither is the matched charge vector [24, 28, 27]. Omitting axis sums all nine entries to 252. Establish the intended shape before reducing.

topics.title: boolean indexing
topics.explanation: A boolean mask is an array of True/False selections. For matched costs [24, 28, 27], costs >= 27 is [False, True, True], so costs[costs >= 27] returns [28, 27]. Boolean indexing creates a copy when reading selected values; direct assignment such as costs[mask] = 0 still updates costs. Filtering expensive rentals is useful for inspection, but dropping invalid rates would misalign the billing inputs.

topics.title: views versus copies
topics.explanation: A view shares underlying storage; a copy has separate storage. With float64 rates [12, 7, 9], trial = rates[:2] followed by trial[0] = 0 changes rates to [0, 7, 9]. Start again and use trial = rates[:2].copy() before editing: rates remains [12, 7, 9]. Basic slices are views; advanced indexing reads are copies. Do not assume every reshape copies the data.

topics.title: vectorization
topics.explanation: Vectorization expresses repeated numeric work as array operations such as days * rates instead of a Python loop over bookings. It can reduce Python-level overhead, but this preview measures no speedup. A pairwise mistake can allocate n × n results rather than n. Keep a loop baseline, validate inputs before either path, and measure time and memory on a stated workload before making performance claims.

sources.title: NUMPY · NumPy 2.3: sum and axis reductions
NUMPY · NumPy 2.3: indexing, including boolean masks
MATH · D2L: linear algebra and reductions (conceptual reading)

steps: Open labs/data-foundations/README.md in the repository or the runnable data-lab download. Follow its Python 3.12 environment and test commands; it pins NumPy 2.3.5. That existing lab has a separate four-rental fixture totalling 103 units. The three-rental SYNTHETIC starter below is an additional exercise, with expected total 79; do not confuse the two datasets.

Save the starter as rental_costs.py in your own practice directory. Implement vectorized_costs using the documented contract. Compare all three costs and the total with the loop and [24, 28, 27], using rtol=0 and atol=1e-9. Inject rates of shape (2,), days of shape (3, 1), and NaN or infinite rates; each must raise ValueError. Restore the original inputs and rerun.

Demonstrate rates[:2] mutating its parent, then repeat from fresh inputs with rates[:2].copy() and prove the parent is unchanged. Record Python/NumPy versions, input values, matched and failed results, and your decision note. State that the fixture is synthetic, not learner-validated or a performance benchmark; billing identity, taxes, discounts and currency rounding remain outside this exercise.

# SYNTHETIC fixture; fictional currency units. Python 3.12 / NumPy 2.3.5.

import numpy as np

DAYS = np.array([2, 4, 3], dtype=np.int64)
RATES = np.array([12, 7, 9], dtype=np.float64)
EXPECTED = np.array([24, 28, 27], dtype=np.float64)
ATOL = 1e-9  # fictional currency units; relative tolerance is zero

    if days.ndim != 1 or rates.ndim != 1 or days.shape != rates.shape:
        raise ValueError("expected equal one-dimensional shapes")
    if not np.isfinite(days).all() or not np.isfinite(rates).all():
        raise ValueError("days and rates must be finite")
    return np.array([float(days[i]) * float(rates[i])
                     for i in range(len(days))])


def vectorized_costs(days, rates):
    # TODO: enforce the same shape and finite-value contract, then multiply.

baseline = loop_costs(DAYS, RATES)
np.testing.assert_allclose(baseline, EXPECTED, rtol=0, atol=ATOL)

orientation: A service contract defines what requests and responses mean. HTTP carries the message, JSON represents data, and application validation checks whether that data is usable.
idea: Receiving a response and receiving valid business data are different successes.
story: The rental desk adds an API that accepts new tickets. A browser sends a request body, but the service cannot assume the body is valid just because bytes arrived. It must parse the document and check the fields before creating a ticket.

One client sends broken JSON; another sends valid JSON with text set to a number. These are different failures. Meera wants an explicit response for each, plus a client that avoids blindly retrying bad input.
example: The body {"text":42} is valid JSON because numbers are allowed. It still violates this endpoint’s contract, which requires a non-empty string. A TypeScript assertion cannot repair that mismatch: the service and client boundary need real checks on the received values.
trap: A 200 response, valid JSON, and a TypeScript type assertion do not each prove the data obeys your contract. Inspect status, structure and meaning separately.

lab.question: At which boundary should this ticket request stop?
lab.limitation: Fixed synthetic case explorer: status codes and gate results are authored for this illustrative API contract. No HTTP requests or TypeScript validation run in this page.

scenarios.label: 1 · Malformed JSON
scenarios.result: Stop before field validation: the JSON document is incomplete.
scenarios.why: Resending the same malformed body does not fix it. The client must correct its serialization.

scenarios.label: 2 · Wrong field type
scenarios.result: JSON parsing succeeds, but application validation rejects the field.
scenarios.why: 422 is this lesson’s documented choice for valid syntax with unusable content; other APIs may document 400.

scenarios.label: 3 · Valid ticket
scenarios.result: The request passes the three shown gates and a ticket is created.
scenarios.why: The response must still be checked by the client. Success status is not permission to assume any arbitrary response shape.

mechanism: Separate transport outcome from response content. A connection failure may leave no response; an HTTP error response is still a response. Parse the body only according to the documented content type and contract.

At the boundary, check field presence, type and relevant constraints. Treat external data as unknown until validation succeeds; a cast tells the compiler what you claim, not what the server actually sent.

Classify recovery by cause and operation. Fix invalid input; handle documented temporary failures with bounded retries only when repeating the operation is safe. A timed-out create may already have committed.

transfer.question: A ticket-create request times out after the server commits. Does the timeout prove no ticket exists?
transfer.answer: No. The client lacks a response, not necessarily a result. Use a documented idempotency or lookup mechanism before repeating the create.

transfer.question: Can every API use exactly the three status choices shown here?
transfer.answer: No. Status semantics come from HTTP, but endpoint contracts choose details within those semantics. Read and test the actual API’s documented errors and versions.

checks.question: Why does {"text":42} fail this endpoint?
options: It violates the required field type
checks.explanation: The syntax is valid; the endpoint requires a string.

checks.question: What does a TypeScript assertion validate at runtime?
checks.explanation: Assertions are removed during compilation and do not check incoming data.

checks.question: What is the safe inference after a create timeout?
checks.explanation: A lost response cannot by itself distinguish failure before work from success before the response was lost.

topics.title: HTTP
topics.explanation: HTTP defines request methods, response status semantics and other message rules. A timeout and a received error status represent different observations; neither should be flattened into a generic empty response.

topics.title: JSON
topics.explanation: JSON encodes values such as objects, arrays, strings and numbers. Parsing {"text":42} produces structured data, but says nothing about whether 42 is an acceptable ticket description.

topics.title: status codes
topics.explanation: Status codes summarize the response semantics. This lesson uses 400 for malformed input, 422 for semantically invalid content and 201 for creation; document the choices your endpoint actually implements.

topics.title: API versioning
topics.explanation: Versioning makes incompatible contract changes explicit. If text is renamed to description, retain compatibility or expose a documented new contract instead of silently breaking older clients.

topics.title: TypeScript boundaries
topics.explanation: TypeScript types help reason about known values during development. Treat network data as unknown and validate it before narrowing; writing value as Ticket does not add a runtime check.

steps: Write an endpoint contract with method, path, required fields, successful response and three explicit error cases.
Run the starter against a string, numeric text and missing text; compare parsing with field validation. Add an incompatible-version fixture.
Describe recovery for malformed input and for a timeout after possible creation. State which repetition guarantees your endpoint would need.

orientation: Concurrency lets work overlap while tasks wait. A task is a scheduled unit of async work; a concurrency limit controls how many may use a scarce resource at once.
idea: Bound active work and release its slot when a request completes or is cancelled.
story: Five rental tickets need a response from a slow mock provider. Starting all five together seems fast, but the provider has capacity for only two active requests. Meera needs a waiting area as well as an active-work limit.

When a customer closes the page, their active request should stop consuming local capacity. Cleanup releases the slot so another ticket can proceed. Cancellation does not prove that a remote provider has undone work already accepted.
example: With five arrived tickets and two slots, two requests are active and three wait. Cancel one active request and finish its cleanup; the next waiting request enters. The new snapshot has two active, two waiting and one cancelled request. The total still accounts for all five.
trap: A semaphore limits entry to a protected section; it does not automatically limit how many tasks you create. A large waiting population can still exhaust memory.

lab.question: Where are the five requests when capacity is limited to two?
lab.limitation: Fixed synthetic case explorer: counts are predetermined scheduling snapshots, not a running event loop, timing benchmark or proof of remote cancellation.

scenarios.label: 1 · Two slots
scenarios.result: The active count stays at two while three requests wait.
scenarios.why: The limit protects active access. A production design must also bound the queue and choose what happens when it is full.

scenarios.label: 2 · No active limit
scenarios.result: All five become active despite the assumed capacity of two.
scenarios.why: Concurrency is not free capacity. This snapshot demonstrates overload risk, not a measured failure probability.

scenarios.label: 3 · Cancel + cleanup
scenarios.result: Cleanup makes the freed slot available to another request.
scenarios.why: Propagate cancellation after cleanup. Releasing local capacity is distinct from confirming a remote side effect stopped.

mechanism: Async code makes progress when a task yields while waiting. A blocking sleep or long synchronous calculation inside the event-loop thread can prevent other tasks from progressing.
Use a bounded queue to control waiting work and a semaphore or fixed worker pool to control active work. Define a full-queue policy such as reject, wait within a deadline or reduce admission.

Put resource cleanup in finally blocks or async context managers. A timeout should trigger a deliberate cancellation path; swallowing cancellation can leave work running longer than the caller expects.

transfer.question: You create a million tasks behind a semaphore of two. Is memory use bounded to two requests?
transfer.answer: No. Only active access is bounded. The waiting tasks still exist; use bounded admission or a queue with a fixed worker pool.

transfer.question: A local task is cancelled. Can you promise a remote email was not sent?
transfer.answer: No. Local cancellation does not establish the provider’s outcome. A side-effecting operation needs a separate reconciliation or deduplication design.

checks.question: What does a two-slot semaphore directly bound?
options: Active entries to its protected section
checks.explanation: Its scope is the code using that semaphore, not all tasks or other service instances.

checks.question: What should cleanup do after cancellation?
options: Release resources and usually propagate cancellation
checks.explanation: Cleanup prevents leaks; propagation lets callers and structured concurrency observe cancellation.

checks.question: Why can async code still stall?
options: Blocking work can occupy the event-loop thread
All async code is automatically parallel
Every await creates a new process
checks.explanation: Async overlap depends on yielding; it does not make arbitrary synchronous work non-blocking.

topics.title: asyncio
topics.explanation: asyncio coordinates asynchronous Python work, commonly around I/O waits. It does not turn a CPU-heavy loop into parallel computation simply because the surrounding function uses async def.

topics.title: tasks
topics.explanation: A task schedules a coroutine so it can make progress with other work. Keep track of task lifetimes and failures; creating unlimited tasks can consume memory even behind a semaphore.

topics.title: timeouts
topics.explanation: A timeout sets a waiting boundary for an operation or caller. Expiration can trigger cancellation, but cleanup may take time and a remote operation may already have produced an effect.

topics.title: cancellation
topics.explanation: Cancellation asks a task to stop at a cancellation opportunity. Use finally or async with for cleanup, and normally propagate CancelledError after cleanup so the caller sees the cancellation.

topics.title: queues
topics.explanation: A bounded queue limits waiting items and exposes overload at admission. A semaphore and queue solve different problems: active access versus waiting backlog.

topics.title: streaming
topics.explanation: Streaming delivers pieces before the whole result is complete. Treat partial output separately from a successful final result, and close the stream when the caller cancels or the deadline expires.

steps: Use the starter around a mocked awaitable provider; instrument entry and exit to record active requests. Run five tasks and verify the observed maximum is two.
Cancel an active task and verify its exit cleanup runs and another request can enter. Include a test that fails if the active counter leaks.
Replace unlimited task creation with a bounded queue and fixed workers. Document the full-queue and partial-stream policies.
practice.starter:
import asyncio

slots = asyncio.Semaphore(2)

async def request(ticket_id):
    async with slots:
        try:
            await asyncio.sleep(0.1)  # mocked I/O wait
            return ticket_id
        finally:
            print("leaving slot", ticket_id)

# Run inside an async main; record active counts and test cancellation.

orientation: A database transaction groups writes into one committed change or no committed change. Tests check that intended behaviour, including failures, using repeatable fixtures.
idea: Keep related writes atomic, and handle duplicate requests separately from rollback.
story: Creating a rental-support ticket requires both a ticket row and an audit row. If the process fails between them, a half-written record can confuse the next person investigating the case. Meera wraps the two writes in one transaction.

A different failure happens after commit: the response never reaches the browser. The rows are safely stored, but the customer clicks submit again. Atomic writes did not prevent that duplicate request; the service also needs a stable request key and a defined repeat policy.
example: A transaction inserts ticket T7 and its audit event. Failure before commit rolls both back. If commit succeeds but the response is lost, both rows remain. Repeating request key K7 should find or reuse the existing logical request, rather than create a second ticket.
trap: Rollback and duplicate prevention solve different problems. A transaction cannot tell a disconnected client whether commit happened, and it does not automatically deduplicate a retry.

lab.question: Which rows remain when ticket creation fails at different points?
lab.limitation: Fixed synthetic case explorer: table counts are authored snapshots of the stated transaction semantics. This page does not run SQL or test a database.

scenarios.label: 1 · Separate writes
scenarios.result: A ticket remains without its required audit row.
scenarios.why: Each write committed independently, so the second failure cannot roll back the earlier committed insert.

scenarios.label: 2 · One transaction
scenarios.result: Neither row is committed.
scenarios.why: The failed transaction is rolled back as a unit. The application must report failure and handle the connection state correctly.

scenarios.label: 3 · Lost response
scenarios.result: Both rows exist even though the client sees a timeout.
scenarios.why: Use the same non-null unique request key and documented retry handling to avoid a second logical ticket.

mechanism: Define the invariant first: every committed ticket creation has its matching audit event. Group the database writes that must preserve that invariant into one transaction.

Give retryable create requests a stable key and enforce uniqueness in the database. Reusing a key with different content needs a conflict policy; a key is not permission to silently overwrite an existing request.

Test failure points, not just the happy path. Inspect committed rows after rollback, duplicate submission and lost-response recovery, then run those tests automatically when the relevant code changes.

transfer.question: A ticket joins to three audit events. Must the joined result contain only one row because there is one ticket?
transfer.answer: No. A join can produce one row per matching event. Aggregate or select deliberately before counting tickets, and test one-to-many fixtures.

transfer.question: The database transaction rolls back. Does it also unsend an email already sent inside the operation?
transfer.answer: No. A separate email provider is outside the database transaction. External effects need a separate delivery and recovery design.

checks.question: What preserves the ticket-plus-audit invariant on an intermediate failure?
checks.explanation: Related writes must share the atomic boundary; speed and indexing do not supply atomicity.

checks.question: What can a lost response after commit mean?
options: The data exists although the client is unsure
checks.explanation: The commit and delivery of its response are separate events.

checks.question: What should a duplicate request key enforce?
options: A fresh key on every retry
checks.explanation: Stable keys let the service recognize a repeated logical request; conflicting payloads require explicit handling.

topics.title: SQL joins
topics.explanation: Joins combine matching rows from tables. One ticket with three audit events can produce three joined rows, so COUNT(*) may count events rather than distinct tickets.

topics.title: transactions
topics.explanation: Transactions group changes under a commit or rollback boundary. They protect database changes inside that boundary, not arbitrary external API calls or messages.

topics.title: indexes
topics.explanation: Indexes can speed selected lookups but add storage and write work. A unique index or constraint can enforce a request-key invariant; an ordinary index alone does not prevent duplicates.

topics.title: tests
topics.explanation: Tests compare observed behaviour with explicit expectations. Include failures before commit, repeated keys and lost responses, because a passing happy-path insert cannot demonstrate recovery.

topics.title: fixtures
topics.explanation: Fixtures provide known starting data and expected outcomes. Include a ticket with multiple audit events and reset state between cases so hidden leftovers do not make tests misleading.

topics.title: CI
topics.explanation: Continuous integration runs chosen checks automatically on repository events. A green run means those checks passed in that environment; it does not prove untested production behaviour.

steps: In a disposable PostgreSQL database, create the two starter tables. Insert a ticket and its audit row in one transaction, then inspect both tables.
Repeat with an intentional failure before commit and verify rollback leaves neither row. Retry a committed key and verify the uniqueness constraint prevents another ticket.
Add one ticket with three audit rows and test your join count. Record the client behaviour expected after a lost commit response.

orientation: Optimization adjusts a parameter to reduce a loss, a number that measures an error. A derivative tells us the local slope; the learning rate controls the size of an update.
idea: A downhill direction helps only when the step size is suitable.
story: Meera tries a tiny model that predicts the same preparation time for every rental ticket. For one training example, the target is 3 hours. The parameter w is the model’s guess, and the squared error is L(w) = (w − 3)².

Starting at 0 hours, the slope is negative, so moving right reduces the error at first. But “move right” is not enough instruction. A small step makes progress; an oversized step crosses the target and can leave an even larger error.
example: At w = 0, the derivative is 2(w − 3) = −6. With learning rate 0.1, the update is w_new = 0 − 0.1 × (−6) = 0.6. Loss falls from 9 to (0.6 − 3)² = 5.76. Subtracting a negative slope moves right.
trap: A negative gradient direction does not make every step safe. A large learning rate can increase loss, and low training loss does not establish good predictions on new tickets.

lab.question: Starting at w = 0, what happens after one gradient step toward the target of 3 hours?
lab.limitation: Fixed synthetic case explorer: these are precomputed one-step calculations for L(w) = (w − 3)², not live training or a guarantee for other objectives.

scenarios.label: 1 · Small step
scenarios.result: The loss decreases, but the estimate is still short of the target.
scenarios.why: This step moves in the helpful direction without travelling far. Further steps would be needed for this rate.

scenarios.label: 2 · Exact toy step
scenarios.result: This particular quadratic reaches its minimum in one step.
scenarios.why: The rate 0.5 works exactly because of this chosen function’s curvature. It is not a universal best learning rate.

scenarios.label: 3 · Overshoot
scenarios.result: The step crosses the target and makes the error worse.
scenarios.why: The direction was locally useful, but the step was too large. Repeated updates at this rate diverge for this quadratic.

mechanism: Separate the objective from the update rule. Here the objective is squared error on one example; it is deliberately simple enough to calculate by hand. Real training objectives may aggregate many examples.
Differentiate to obtain 2(w − 3), then subtract learning rate times that slope. In several dimensions, the gradient collects one partial derivative per parameter and the same update idea applies.

Check both the calculation and the outcome. A finite-difference approximation can expose a wrong analytic gradient, while held-out examples test whether reducing this training objective helps the actual task.

transfer.question: At w = 5, the slope is +4. With rate 0.1, does the next value move left or right?
transfer.answer: Left: 5 − 0.1 × 4 = 4.6. It moves toward 3 in this example because the positive slope is subtracted.

transfer.question: Does the rate 0.5 reaching zero loss here prove it is a good rate for a neural network?
transfer.answer: No. This is a one-parameter quadratic with known curvature. Other scales, objectives and model geometries change suitable step sizes.

checks.question: What is the slope of (w − 3)² at w = 0?
checks.explanation: The derivative is 2(w − 3); substitute zero to get −6.

checks.question: Why did rate 1.1 increase loss?
checks.explanation: A locally downhill direction can become harmful when the step is too large.

checks.question: What does lower training loss alone establish?
checks.explanation: Correct implementation and usefulness on new data require additional checks.

topics.title: derivatives
topics.explanation: A derivative measures the local rate of change of a scalar function. For squared error, 2(w − 3) says which direction initially raises loss; it does not describe every distant point.

topics.title: gradients
topics.explanation: A gradient is the vector of partial derivatives with respect to several parameters. If a model has a slope and an intercept, each receives an update based on its own derivative.

topics.title: chain rule
topics.explanation: The chain rule tracks derivatives through composed operations. Writing u = w − 3 and L = u² gives dL/dw = (2u) × 1, making the dependency explicit.

topics.title: numerical stability
topics.explanation: Finite-precision arithmetic can distort a mathematically valid calculation. A finite-difference step that is too tiny can lose useful digits when nearly equal losses are subtracted; compare several sensible step sizes.

topics.title: learning rate
topics.explanation: The learning rate scales the gradient update. Its useful size depends on the objective and parameter scale, so a rate that works for this toy loss is not a general recipe.

sources.title: Dive into Deep Learning: gradient descent

steps: Run the starter for rates 0.1, 0.5 and 1.1, recording five updates and losses for each. Explain the sign of the first step.
At w = 1, compare the analytic derivative with central finite differences for h = 0.1, 0.0001 and 1e-12. Record differences without assuming smaller h is always better.
Change the target or rescale the loss and repeat. State why this demonstration does not measure generalization to new rental tickets.

orientation: Conditional probability asks how likely an event is after some information is known. A base rate is how common the event was before that new information.
idea: An alert’s meaning depends on both detector behaviour and how common the underlying problem is.
story: Meera’s desk tests an urgent-ticket detector. It flags 90% of truly urgent tickets, which sounds reassuring. But she needs a different answer: among the tickets it flags, how many actually need the urgent queue?

The two questions reverse the condition. When urgent tickets are rare, even a modest false-alert rate can produce many more false alarms than true ones. Count both groups before interpreting a positive flag.
example: Among 1,000 tickets, suppose 10 are urgent. The detector catches 9 of them. Of the remaining 990 routine tickets, it incorrectly flags 99. Only 9 of 108 flagged tickets are urgent: about 8.3%, despite catching 90% of urgent cases.
trap: “Flags 90% of urgent cases” is not “90% of flags are urgent”. The first conditions on true urgency; the second conditions on receiving a flag.

lab.question: With the same detector rates, how does the urgent-ticket base rate change the meaning of a flag?
lab.limitation: Fixed synthetic case explorer: each cohort has 1,000 tickets, a 90% true-positive rate and a 10% false-positive rate by assumption. These are invented counts, not calibrated model measurements.

scenarios.label: 1 · Rare urgency
scenarios.result: Most flags are false alarms in this rare-urgency cohort.
scenarios.why: The routine group is 99 times larger than the urgent group. Ten percent of it contributes many false flags.

scenarios.label: 2 · More urgency
scenarios.result: Half the flags are urgent, with unchanged detector rates.
scenarios.why: Changing the population changes the posterior meaning of the flag, even when sensitivity and false-positive rate stay fixed.

scenarios.label: 3 · Urgency common
scenarios.result: Now nine out of ten flags are urgent.
scenarios.why: This improvement comes from a changed base rate in the toy population, not a better detector.

mechanism: Draw the whole population before computing percentages. Split tickets into urgent and routine groups, then apply the flag rate separately to each group. This keeps the denominators visible.

Collect every flag and divide true alerts by all alerts. Bayes’ rule expresses the same bookkeeping algebraically: posterior probability depends on the prior base rate and the likelihood of the observed flag.

Separate this population calculation from a model’s self-reported confidence. Interpreting a score as a probability requires calibration evidence on relevant data, and a population change can weaken that interpretation.

transfer.question: A detector moves from a specialist breakdown queue to all customer messages. Its flag rates stay fixed, but urgency is rarer. What happens to urgent cases among flags?
transfer.answer: The fraction decreases under these assumptions because routine tickets contribute a larger share of false alerts. Recalculate with the new base rate.

transfer.question: Does a model output of 0.9 guarantee this individual ticket is urgent?
transfer.answer: No. Even a well-calibrated 0.9 group contains some non-urgent cases. Calibration describes frequencies over relevant groups, not certainty about one example.

checks.question: Which denominator gives urgent cases among flags?
checks.explanation: The question conditions on receiving a flag, so use true plus false alerts.

checks.question: What changed between the three lab cases?
checks.explanation: The cohort size and both detector rates stay fixed; the urgent population share changes.

checks.question: What does good calibration mean approximately?
options: Among cases scored near 0.8, about 80% are positive
The model never encounters new populations
checks.explanation: Calibration compares score groups with observed frequencies on relevant data.

topics.title: conditional probability
topics.explanation: P(flag | urgent) describes flags among urgent tickets; P(urgent | flag) describes urgency among flags. Reversing the condition changes the denominator and usually the answer.

topics.title: Bayes
topics.explanation: Bayes’ rule updates a prior probability using evidence. The count-based example computes the same posterior without hiding the false alarms in a formula.

topics.title: expectation
topics.explanation: An expectation is a probability-weighted average of possible values. If a fictional error costs 10 units with probability 0.2 and zero otherwise, its expected cost is 2 units, not a promise about the next case.

topics.title: entropy
topics.explanation: Entropy summarizes uncertainty in a probability distribution. A 50/50 binary distribution has more entropy than a 90/10 distribution, but low entropy does not prove a forecast is accurate.

topics.title: cross-entropy
topics.explanation: Cross-entropy penalizes probabilities assigned to observed outcomes. Assigning only 0.1 probability to the event that occurs incurs a larger log loss than assigning 0.9; confident mistakes are costly under this score.

topics.title: KL divergence
topics.explanation: KL divergence measures a directional discrepancy between distributions and is not generally symmetric. It is zero for matching distributions under the usual assumptions; a small value does not by itself establish business usefulness.

sources.title: Dive into Deep Learning: information theory

steps: Recreate the three cohorts with the starter and verify true-alert, false-alert and posterior calculations by hand.
Change the false-positive rate while holding prevalence fixed. Explain which quantity you changed and which denominator stays relevant.
Write a short release note distinguishing measured detector rates, assumed prevalence and unverified calibration. Do not describe the fixture as production accuracy.
practice.starter:
total, sensitivity, false_positive_rate = 1000, 0.9, 0.1
for prevalence in (0.01, 0.1, 0.5):
    urgent = total * prevalence
    true_alerts = urgent * sensitivity
    false_alerts = (total - urgent) * false_positive_rate
    posterior = true_alerts / (true_alerts + false_alerts)
    print(prevalence, true_alerts, false_alerts, posterior)

orientation: An experiment compares alternatives using observations. Sampling uncertainty means the observed difference can change when a different set of cases is drawn; paired comparison keeps both systems attached to the same case.
idea: A small observed win needs uncertainty and sampling context before it supports a release.
story: Meera compares two routing systems on the same 20 rental tickets. A gets 14 right and B gets 16 right. The apparent gain is 10 percentage points, but the team should inspect which tickets account for that difference.

B alone is correct on four tickets; A alone is correct on two. On fourteen, they tie. If this tiny sample had included different cases, the gain could change. Resampling paired rows makes that sensitivity visible without pretending to collect new evidence.
example: The per-ticket difference is +1 when only B is correct, −1 when only A is correct and 0 for ties. Four +1 values, two −1 values and fourteen zeros give (4 − 2) / 20 = 0.10, a 10-percentage-point gain for B.
trap: Resampling the same 20 cases thousands of times does not create thousands of independent observations. It explores variability conditional on the original sample.

lab.question: Can selected resamples of the same paired tickets change the apparent winner?
lab.limitation: Fixed synthetic case explorer: the page shows an original 20-row fixture and two deliberately selected valid resamples. It does not run a bootstrap or estimate a confidence interval from these three snapshots.

scenarios.label: 1 · Original sample
scenarios.result: B leads by 10 percentage points on the original fixture.
scenarios.why: Every row retains both A and B outcomes. The net gain is (4 − 2) divided by 20.

scenarios.label: 2 · Resample A
scenarios.result: This possible resample favours A by 5 percentage points.
scenarios.why: Sampling with replacement repeats some rows and omits others. A single selected resample is not an estimate of how often A wins.

scenarios.label: 3 · Resample B
scenarios.result: Another possible resample favours B by 25 percentage points.
scenarios.why: Both selected resamples are compatible with the original rows. A full procedure uses many random resamples and stated assumptions, not cherry-picked examples.

mechanism: Pair outcomes by ticket before subtracting. This controls which case each score came from and reveals wins, losses and ties that two aggregate percentages hide.

For a paired bootstrap, sample row indices with replacement and use the same indices for both systems. Recompute the mean difference for each resample; independently shuffling A and B destroys the pairing.

Interpret uncertainty alongside practical value and data quality. A narrow interval on a biased sample can still mislead, while related tickets may require resampling whole customer groups rather than treating rows as independent.

transfer.question: Someone duplicates every benchmark ticket ten times. Does the apparent sample size of 200 provide ten times as much independent evidence?
transfer.answer: No. It still contains only 20 unique cases. Treating duplicates as independent can make uncertainty look artificially small.

transfer.question: A confidence interval includes zero. Does that prove the systems are equally good?
transfer.answer: No. It means the procedure and data have not separated a zero difference from other compatible effects at that level. More informative data or a planned equivalence analysis may be needed.

checks.question: What must stay together in a paired bootstrap?
options: Both systems’ outcomes for the same ticket
checks.explanation: Resampling whole pairs preserves the shared-case comparison.

checks.question: What is the original gain in the fixture?
checks.explanation: Two extra correct outcomes divided by 20 is 0.10, or 10 percentage points.

checks.question: Why keep a final test set untouched during model selection?
options: To reduce selection based on the test answers
checks.explanation: Repeatedly choosing models on test results can overfit that test set; an untouched test is still not a production guarantee.

topics.title: sampling
topics.explanation: A sample is a selected subset of the population of interest. Twenty routine English tickets cannot establish behaviour for all languages or urgent breakdowns, regardless of how carefully their average is computed.

topics.title: confidence intervals
topics.explanation: A confidence interval comes from a procedure with a repeated-sampling coverage interpretation under assumptions. It is not a statement that a fixed interval has a specified probability of containing a fixed true effect.

topics.title: bootstrap
topics.explanation: Bootstrap resamples observed data with replacement to approximate variability of a statistic. Small, biased or dependent samples can make naive intervals unreliable; the two selected resamples here do not constitute an interval.

topics.title: paired tests
topics.explanation: Paired comparisons analyse related observations together, such as both systems on the same ticket. Appropriate paired tests use the within-pair differences and their assumptions, rather than pretending the systems saw unrelated cases.

topics.title: power
topics.explanation: Power describes how often a planned test detects a specified effect under stated assumptions. Failure to find a clear difference may reflect limited information, so decide the smallest useful effect and data needs before collecting results.

topics.title: multiple comparisons
topics.explanation: Trying many candidates and reporting only the largest observed gain invites selection noise. Use validation for selection, preserve final evaluation data and account for the planned comparison procedure rather than repeatedly peeking for a win.

steps: Construct the twenty paired outcomes described above and verify the observed 10-point gain. Keep ticket IDs attached to both systems.
Run the seeded starter to obtain an illustrative percentile interval. Explain that this tiny fixture and simple method do not establish reliable population coverage.

Write a release decision that states practical gain, uncertainty, sampling limitations and an untouched final-evaluation plan. Identify any repeated-customer groups before choosing a real resampling unit.
practice.starter:
import random

# B correctness minus A correctness, one value per paired ticket.
differences = [0]*12 + [1]*4 + [-1]*2 + [0]*2
rng = random.Random(7)
n = len(differences)
gains = sorted(sum(rng.choices(differences, k=n))/n
               for _ in range(2000))
print("observed percentage-point gain", 100*sum(differences)/n)
print("illustrative percentile endpoints", 100*gains[50], 100*gains[1949])
# A teaching approximation, not a small-sample coverage guarantee.
